overview.title: From layers to models: topology as hypothesis space
overview.chapter: 3 Introduction to TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX, and Keras
overview.main_topic: What the base Layer.__call__() does besides shape inference, the Keras Model class as a graph of layers, common network topologies, and why architecture choice defines the hypothesis space.
overview.central_idea: A model is a graph of layers, and choosing its topology restricts learning to a specific family of tensor operations; training then only searches for good weight values inside that family. The architecture therefore encodes your prior assumptions about the problem.
overview.importance: This page moves from single layers to whole models and gives the conceptual reason architecture matters so much: it fixes what can be learned at all. The idea of architecture as a hypothesis space returns throughout the book (for example, ConvNet design in chapter 9, p.292).
learning_objectives: Know that Layer.__call__() handles shape inference, eager/graph routing and masking, and that your own forward-pass code goes in call().
Describe the Keras Model class as a graph of layers and Sequential as its simplest subclass.
Name common non-sequential topologies: two-branch networks, multihead networks, residual connections.
Know the two ways to build complex models in Keras: subclassing Model and the Functional API (chapter 7).
Explain how a network topology defines a hypothesis space and encodes prior assumptions, using the single-Dense-layer/linear-separability example.
prerequisites: The SimpleDense layer and its build()/call() methods (p.118-119)
The definition of machine learning as searching a space of possibilities guided by feedback (chapter 1)
Affine transformations and the Dense layer (chapter 2)

summary:
The page begins by finishing the `keras.Sequential` example from p.119, whose final layer is `SimpleDense(10, activation="softmax")`. Thanks to automatic shape inference, none of the `SimpleDense` layers needs to be told its input size.

The authors then point out that shape inference is **not the only job** of the base `Layer.__call__()` method. It also routes between **eager** and **graph** execution and handles **input masking** (covered in chapter 14). The practical rule: when you write your own layer, put the forward pass in `call()`, never in `__call__()`.

Section **3.6.3 From layers to models** says that a deep learning model is a **graph of layers**, represented in Keras by the `Model` class. So far you have only seen `Sequential` models, a subclass of `Model` that is a simple stack mapping one input to one output. Many other topologies exist: **two-branch networks**, **multihead networks** and **residual connections**. Figure 3.5 (on p.121) shows how complex the graph of a Transformer is. Keras offers two ways to build such models: **subclassing `Model`** or the **Functional API**. Both are covered in chapter 7.

The key conceptual point is that **the topology of a model defines a hypothesis space**. Recalling chapter 1's definition of machine learning as "searching for useful representations of some input data, within a predefined space of possibilities, using guidance from a feedback signal", the authors explain that picking a topology restricts the space of possibilities to a specific series of tensor operations. Training then only searches for good values of the weight tensors in those operations. To learn from data you must make assumptions about it, so **the architecture encodes your prior knowledge**. For example, a two-class classifier made of a single `Dense` layer with no activation (a pure affine transformation) assumes the two classes are **linearly separable**.

The page ends by saying that choosing an architecture is more art than science. There are best practices, but only practice makes you a good "neural network architect". The next chapters will teach both explicit principles and intuition (the sentence continues on p.121).

paragraphs.excerpt: Note that automatic shape inference is not the only thing that the
paragraphs.what_it_says: The base Layer class's __call__() method does more than infer shapes. It also handles routing between eager and graph execution and input masking (chapter 14). Rule of thumb: when implementing a layer, put the forward pass in call().
paragraphs.what_it_means: On p.119 the authors showed a simplified __call__() that builds the weights on first use and then delegates to call(). The real one is a wrapper that does extra bookkeeping around your code. If you override __call__() yourself, you lose all of it: lazy weight creation, the backend's choice of eager or compiled execution, and propagation of masks for padded sequences. By overriding only call(), you write the pure computation and let the framework take care of everything around it.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the standard contract for custom Keras layers: __init__ for configuration, build() for state (weights), call() for computation. Breaking it leads to subtle bugs, for example layers that fail inside compiled training loops or ignore masks.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Template-method pattern: the framework-owned __call__() is the fixed outer algorithm (check built, build, set up execution context, handle masks, call), and the user-overridable call() is the hook.

Marking some timesteps of a sequence (typically padding) to be ignored by downstream layers; covered in chapter 14.
The method in which a custom layer defines its forward computation.

paragraphs.excerpt: A deep learning model is a graph of layers. In Keras, that's
paragraphs.what_it_says: A model is a graph of layers, represented by the Keras Model class. Sequential, the only kind seen so far, is a subclass of Model that stacks layers linearly, mapping one input to one output. Many other topologies will come up, including two-branch networks, multihead networks and residual connections. The short follow-up paragraph (p120_e11) adds that topologies can get very involved, pointing to figure 3.5's Transformer, an architecture designed for text.
paragraphs.what_it_means: 'Graph' here means a directed acyclic graph: nodes are layers (or layer outputs) and edges carry tensors. A Sequential model is the special case where the graph is a chain. In a two-branch network, two inputs or two processing paths are merged. A multihead network produces several outputs from a shared trunk. A residual connection adds a block's input back to its output, so the graph contains a shortcut edge. None of these can be written as a plain list of layers, which is why more general model-building tools are needed.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It tells you that Sequential is a convenience for the simplest case, not the general form of a model. Most real architectures (ResNets, Transformers, multimodal models) are non-linear graphs.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Model is itself a kind of Layer (a composite layer) that adds training-related methods; Sequential is a Model whose graph is a linear chain.

paragraphs.excerpt: There are generally two ways of building such models in Keras:
paragraphs.what_it_says: Keras gives two ways to build non-sequential models: subclass the Model class directly, or use the Functional API, which 'lets you do more with less code'. Both are covered in chapter 7.
paragraphs.what_it_means: With subclassing, you write a Python class with layers created in __init__ and a call() method, just like the custom-layer pattern on p.118. With the Functional API, you call layers on symbolic input tensors and Keras records the resulting graph of layers as an explicit data structure. Chapter 7 (p.216) adds that the Functional API is the most commonly used of the three APIs, while subclassing gives full control at the cost of losing some built-in features.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It previews a design choice you will make for every non-trivial model: an explicit, inspectable graph (Functional) or arbitrary Python code (subclassing).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Functional models are data structures you can inspect (summary, plot_model, feature extraction); subclassed models are opaque bytecode (p.228).

terminology.meaning: Keras API in which you build a model by calling layers on symbolic tensors, producing an explicit graph of layers.

paragraphs.excerpt: The topology of a model defines a hypothesis space. You may remember
paragraphs.what_it_says: Recalling chapter 1's definition of machine learning, "searching for useful representations of some input data, within a predefined space of possibilities, using guidance from a feedback signal", the authors say that the model's topology is what defines that space (the hypothesis space). Choosing a topology restricts you to a specific series of tensor operations mapping input to output. Learning is then the search for good values of the weight tensors used in those operations.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The architecture fixes the form of the function, and the weights are the free parameters within that form. For example, if the architecture is Dense(32, relu) → Dense(10, softmax), every function the model can ever represent is softmax(W2·relu(W1·x + b1) + b2) for some W1, b1, W2, b2. Gradient descent moves through this parameter space and cannot reach any function outside it. 'Hypothesis space' is the set of all such functions.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It separates the two decisions in deep learning. Humans choose the hypothesis space (architecture). The optimizer chooses a point in it (weights). If the right function is not in the space, no amount of training will find it.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Hypothesis space H = { f_θ : θ ∈ Θ }, where f is fixed by the architecture and θ ranges over all weight values; training selects θ* that minimizes the loss.

terminology.meaning: The set of all input-to-output functions a model can represent as its weights vary; fixed by the architecture.
Chapter 1's phrase for the same idea: the predefined set of candidate transformations that learning searches through.

connections: p.292: chapter 9 restates that architecture choices define the hypothesis space searched by gradient descent

paragraphs.excerpt: To learn from data, you have to make assumptions about it. These
paragraphs.what_it_says: Learning requires assumptions, and those assumptions decide what can be learned. That is why the structure of the hypothesis space, meaning the architecture, is extremely important: it encodes the assumptions and prior knowledge the model starts with. Example: a two-class classifier made of one Dense layer with no activation (a pure affine transformation) assumes the two classes are linearly separable.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A single affine layer computes $w\cdot x + b$. Thresholding that score splits input space with a flat hyperplane $w\cdot x + b = 0$. If the classes can only be separated by a curved boundary (as in XOR, or concentric rings), this model cannot succeed whatever weights it learns. Choosing the architecture amounts to betting that the true decision rule has this shape.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Architecture choice is a form of prior knowledge. Convolutions assume local, translation-invariant patterns (chapter 9, p.292); recurrent and attention layers assume sequential structure. Picking an architecture that matches the data's structure is often what makes deep learning work.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Inductive bias: the built-in assumptions that let a learner generalize beyond its training data. Without some bias, no generalization is possible.

terminology.meaning: Assumptions about the problem that are built into the model before it sees any data.
A linear map plus a translation, W·x + b; what a Dense layer computes before its activation.
Two classes that can be perfectly separated by a hyperplane (a straight line in 2D).

paragraphs.what_it_says: Choosing an architecture is more art than science. There are best practices and principles, but only practice turns you into a 'proper neural network architect'. The next chapters will teach explicit principles and also build intuition about what works for specific problems (the sentence finishes on p.121).
paragraphs.what_it_means: There is no algorithm that takes a dataset and outputs the right architecture. Architecture search methods exist, but practitioners mostly rely on established patterns (residual connections, normalization, attention) and experience. The authors set expectations: you will learn rules of thumb, and judgment comes from building many models.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It frames the rest of the book, which moves from principles (chapters 5-7) to architecture patterns for images, sequences and text (chapters 8 onward).

concepts.name: Keras Layer: __call__() vs call()
concepts.definition: A Keras layer exposes a framework-owned __call__() that wraps the user-defined call(). __call__() handles lazy building (shape inference), routing between eager and graph execution, and masking.
concepts.intuition: call() is the recipe; __call__() is the kitchen staff who check the ingredients are ready, set up the stove and pass along notes before and after you cook.
concepts.technical: On first invocation __call__() calls build(input_shape) and sets built=True (p.119), then calls call(inputs). It also manages backend-specific tracing and mask propagation.
concepts.significance: Correct custom layers depend on overriding call() and not __call__().
concepts.example: class SimpleDense(keras.Layer): build() creates W and b; call() returns activation(inputs @ W + b).
concepts.misconception: Overriding __call__() is equivalent to overriding call(). It is not: you would bypass build-on-first-call, execution routing and masking.

concepts.name: Keras Model as a graph of layers
concepts.definition: The Keras Model class represents a deep learning model as a graph of layers. Sequential is a subclass limited to a linear stack with one input and one output.
concepts.intuition: Layers are LEGO bricks (p.117); a Model is the assembled structure, which may branch and merge rather than being a single tower.
concepts.technical: Model adds training and inference methods (fit, evaluate, predict) on top of layer behaviour (p.227). Non-linear graphs are built with the Functional API or by subclassing Model.
concepts.significance: It is the object you compile, train, save and deploy.
concepts.example: A two-input model that concatenates text features and metadata features before a shared Dense classifier is a Model but not a Sequential.
concepts.misconception: Every Keras model is a Sequential list of layers. Sequential is only the simplest case.

concepts.name: Network topology
concepts.definition: The pattern of connections between layers in a model, e.g. a linear stack, two-branch, multihead, or residual.
concepts.intuition: The wiring diagram of the model, independent of the weight values.
concepts.technical: A directed acyclic graph whose nodes are layers and whose edges carry tensors. Branches join through merge operations (concatenate, add), and heads split from shared nodes.
concepts.significance: It determines which computations are possible and therefore the hypothesis space.
concepts.example: Figure 3.5 (p.121): the Transformer's encoder-decoder graph with attention blocks, residual additions and normalization.
concepts.misconception: Topology is just a code style. In fact it changes which functions the model can represent.

concepts.name: Hypothesis space
concepts.definition: The predefined space of possible input-to-output transformations a model can represent. By choosing a topology, you restrict it to a specific series of tensor operations whose weight values are then learned.
concepts.intuition: The architecture draws the map; training only moves a pin around on it.
concepts.technical: $\mathcal{H} = \{ f_\theta : \theta \in \Theta \}$, where $f$ is fixed by the architecture and $\theta$ is the collection of weight tensors. Training picks $\theta^* = \arg\min_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta)$ (approximately, via gradient descent).
concepts.significance: If the target function is not (approximately) in $\mathcal{H}$, training cannot find it, so architecture design matters a great deal.
concepts.example: A single linear Dense layer for two-class classification: $\mathcal{H}$ contains only hyperplane decision boundaries.
concepts.misconception: A big enough training set lets any model learn anything. Data can only select among the functions the architecture allows.

concepts.name: Architecture as prior knowledge (inductive bias)
concepts.definition: The assumptions about the problem that a model encodes before seeing data. The book calls this 'the prior knowledge that the model starts with'.
concepts.intuition: Choosing a model is choosing what you believe about the world. For instance, 'nearby pixels matter together' leads to convolutions.
concepts.technical: The term 'inductive bias' is standard in machine learning but is not used on this page; the book's phrasing is assumptions/prior knowledge encoded in the hypothesis space.
concepts.significance: Good assumptions make learning feasible from limited data; wrong ones cap performance.
concepts.example: Single affine layer means assuming linear separability; convolution layers mean assuming local, translation-invariant patterns (p.292).
concepts.misconception: Assumptions are bad and models should be assumption-free. Without assumptions nothing can be learned, as the book says.

concepts.name: Linear separability
concepts.definition: Two classes are linearly separable if a hyperplane $w\cdot x + b = 0$ puts all points of one class on one side and all points of the other class on the other side.
concepts.intuition: In 2D: you can draw one straight line between the red and blue dots.
concepts.technical: A single Dense layer with no activation computes an affine score; thresholding it yields exactly the family of hyperplane classifiers.
concepts.significance: It is the assumption made by the simplest linear model and the reason hidden layers with nonlinear activations are needed for harder problems.
concepts.example: AND and OR on binary inputs are linearly separable; XOR is not.
concepts.misconception: Adding more Dense layers without activations fixes non-separability. A stack of affine maps is still affine.

concepts.name: Functional API vs Model subclassing
concepts.definition: The two ways Keras offers to build models beyond Sequential: the Functional API ('do more with less code') and direct subclassing of Model.
concepts.intuition: Functional = drawing the wiring diagram explicitly; subclassing = writing a program that does the wiring.
concepts.technical: Covered in chapter 7 (p.216-228): Functional models are inspectable graphs; subclassed models hide connectivity in call().
concepts.significance: This is the main design decision for complex Keras models.
concepts.misconception: Subclassing is always better because it is more flexible. You give up summary/plot/feature-extraction support (p.228).

math.title: A single Dense layer without activation is an affine map with a hyperplane boundary
math.latex: \hat{y} = w\cdot x + b, \qquad \text{decision boundary: } w\cdot x + b = 0
math.source_text: "a model made of a single Dense layer with no activation (a pure affine transformation)"; the book gives no formula here, this is the formal version of that phrase

variables.meaning: weight vector of the Dense layer (one output unit for a two-class score)
raw score; predict class 1 if positive, class 0 otherwise

math.operations: Dot product of weights and input, plus bias. Thresholding the score at 0 gives the class.
math.purpose: Shows why this architecture assumes linear separability: the set of points where the prediction flips is a flat hyperplane.
math.interpretation: Whatever values training gives $w$ and $b$, the classifier can only cut input space with one straight boundary.
math.intuition: Training can rotate and slide the line, but never bend it.
math.numerical_example: With $w=(1,1)$, $b=-1$: the point $(1,1)$ scores $1>0$ (class 1) and $(0,0)$ scores $-1<0$ (class 0). The boundary is the line $x_1+x_2=1$. For XOR points $(0,0),(1,1)$ in class 0 and $(0,1),(1,0)$ in class 1, no choice of $w,b$ separates them.

deeper.title: Why stacking linear layers does not escape linear separability
deeper.body: Beyond the book: suppose you stack two Dense layers without activations: $h = W_1 x + b_1$, $y = W_2 h + b_2$. Substituting gives $y = (W_2W_1)x + (W_2 b_1 + b_2)$, which is again a single affine map $W'x + b'$. So the hypothesis space of any depth of purely linear layers equals that of one linear layer. Only the nonlinearity (e.g. `relu`) between layers enlarges the hypothesis space beyond hyperplanes. This is the precise reason the book's single-`Dense` example implies linear separability, and why activations matter.

deeper.title: Architecture as a search territory
deeper.body: Think of training as a hiker (gradient descent) searching for the lowest valley. The architecture decides which region of the world the hiker is allowed to explore. Pick a region with no good valleys, for example a linear model for curved data, and the hiker's skill does not matter. Pick a region shaped like the problem, for example convolutions for images, and good solutions are easy to reach.

deeper.title: The three topologies named on the page, concretely
deeper.body:
Note (examples not in the book on this page):
- **Two-branch network**: e.g. a model that takes an image and a text description through separate sub-networks, then concatenates their features.
- **Multihead network**: a shared feature extractor with, say, one head predicting a category (softmax) and another predicting a price (regression).
- **Residual connection**: `y = x + block(x)`. The input skips over a block and is added back, which eases training of deep networks (covered in chapter 9).

None of these fits a single list of layers, which is why `Sequential` is not enough.

takeaways: Layer.__call__() handles shape inference, eager/graph routing and masking; your forward pass belongs in call().
A Keras Model is a graph of layers; Sequential is the special case of a linear stack with one input and one output.
Two-branch, multihead and residual topologies need the Functional API or Model subclassing (chapter 7).

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed on this page as something the base Layer.__call__() takes care of?
options: Routing between eager and graph execution
questions.explanation: The page lists shape inference, eager/graph routing and input masking. The optimizer is chosen in the compile step (section 3.6.4, p.121) and has nothing to do with a layer's __call__().

questions.question: When implementing your own Keras layer, in which method should you put the forward pass?
questions.explanation: The page says: 'when implementing your own layers, put the forward pass in the call() method.' __call__() wraps call() with building and other bookkeeping.

questions.question: What is the relationship between Sequential and Model in Keras?
options: Sequential is a subclass of Model for simple single-input, single-output stacks
Model is a subclass of Sequential
Sequential is a kind of Layer that cannot be trained
questions.answer: Sequential is a subclass of Model for simple single-input, single-output stacks
questions.explanation: The page states that Sequential models are 'a subclass of Model', simple stacks mapping one input to one output. Model is the more general class, so it is not a subclass of Sequential. The two are closely related, and Sequential models are trained like any Model.

questions.question: Explain in your own words how choosing a network topology defines a hypothesis space, and what training then searches for.
questions.answer: The topology fixes a specific series of tensor operations from input to output; the set of all functions obtainable by varying the weights is the hypothesis space. Training searches only for good values of those weight tensors.
questions.explanation: This restates the page's link to chapter 1's definition of ML as searching a predefined space of possibilities. The architecture defines the space and gradient descent searches within it.

questions.question: A two-class classifier consists of a single Dense(1) layer with no activation, followed by thresholding at 0. Can it correctly classify XOR: (0,0)→0, (1,1)→0, (0,1)→1, (1,0)→1? Justify.
questions.answer: No. The model computes w·x + b, whose decision boundary is a straight line, and XOR's classes are not linearly separable.
questions.explanation: To classify (0,1) and (1,0) as positive you need w2 + b > 0 and w1 + b > 0. To classify (0,0) and (1,1) as negative you need b < 0 and w1 + w2 + b < 0. Adding the first two gives w1 + w2 + 2b > 0, so w1 + w2 + b > -b > 0, which contradicts the last inequality. This is the page's linear-separability assumption made concrete.

questions.question: According to the page, what are the two ways to build non-sequential models in Keras?
options: Subclassing Model and the Functional API
questions.answer: Subclassing Model and the Functional API
questions.explanation: The page names directly subclassing Model and the Functional API, both covered in chapter 7. Sequential cannot express non-linear graphs, tf.function/jax.jit are compilation tools, and build()/call() are layer methods.

questions.question: Why does the book say the architecture of a model is 'extremely important'?
questions.answer: Because learning requires assumptions, and the architecture is where they are encoded: it is the prior knowledge the model starts with and it determines what can be learned at all.
questions.explanation: From the paragraph 'To learn from data, you have to make assumptions about it...'. A poorly matched architecture puts the solution outside the hypothesis space.

questions.question: Can you sketch the graph of a multihead network and a residual block, and explain why neither can be written as a plain Sequential list?
questions.answer: Self-check: a multihead network has one trunk feeding several outputs; a residual block has an extra edge adding the input to the block output. Both have nodes with more than one outgoing or incoming edge, which a linear stack cannot represent.
questions.explanation: Sequential maps a single input through a chain to a single output; branching and merging require the Functional API or subclassing.
